{{Ecomodernism}}
'''Stewart Brand''' (born December 14, 1938) is an American project developer and writer, best known as the co-founder and editor of the ''[[Whole Earth Catalog]]''. Other organizations he has founded include [[the WELL]], the [[Global Business Network]], and the [[Long Now Foundation]]. He is the author of several books, most recently ''[[Whole Earth Discipline|Whole Earth Discipline: An Ecopragmatist Manifesto]]'' and ''Maintenance: Of Everything''.

==Life==
Brand was born in [[Rockford, Illinois]], and attended [[Phillips Exeter Academy]] in New Hampshire. He studied [[biology]] at [[Stanford University]] under [[Paul R. Ehrlich]], graduating in 1960.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://oac.cdlib.org/findaid/ark:/13030/kt6199s310/|title=Brand (Stewart) papers – Online Archive of California|work=Online Archive of California}}</ref> As a soldier in the [[U.S.&nbsp;Army]], he was a [[parachutist]] and taught [[infantry]] skills; he later expressed the view that his experience in the military had fostered his competence in organizing.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://bigthink.com/videos/big-think-interview-with-stewart-brand|title=Big Think Interview with Stewart Brand – Big Think|author=Stewart Brand|work=Big Think}}</ref>

A civilian again in 1962, he moved back to California, where he has mostly lived since. He studied design at [[San Francisco Art Institute]], photography at [[San Francisco State College]], and participated in a scientific study of then-legal [[LSD]] with [[Myron Stolaroff]]'s International Foundation for Advanced Study, in [[Menlo Park, California]].<ref>Markoff, John 2022 Whole Earth: The Many Lives of Stewart Brand. New York:Penguin, pp. 77–79</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Kennedy |first=Pagan |title=Inventology: How we dream up things that change the world |publisher=Mariner Books |year=2016 |isbn=9780544811928 |location=Boston |pages=126, 130}}</ref>

Brand became acquainted with [[Richard Raymond (publisher)|Richard Raymond]], a land-use and community-development expert turned entrepreneur, who had established a nonprofit society, the [[Portola Institute]] in Menlo Park. Raymond had become a consultant to the [[Warm Springs Indian Reservation]] and recommended Brand for a job there as a photographer.<ref name="brandlife">{{cite book |last1=Markoff |first1=John |title=Whole Earth: The Many Lives of Stewart Brand |date=2022 |publisher=Penguin |location=New York |isbn=9780735223943 |edition=first}}</ref>

In 1966, Brand married the [[mathematician]] Lois Jennings,<ref name="CHM/102792664" /> a half-[[Odawa]]<ref>{{cite magazine |title=Stewart Brand Saw the Future |url=https://newrepublic.com/article/166740/stewart-brand-whole-earth-catalog-saw-future |magazine=[[The New Republic]] |access-date=March 25, 2025 |date=June 14, 2022}}</ref> [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native American]].{{sfn|Brand|2009|p=236}} The couple divorced in 1973.<ref name="CHM/102792664">{{multiref2
|{{cite web |title=Lois Britton (née Jennings) oral history |url=https://www.computerhistory.org/collections/catalog/102792664 |website=[[computerhistory.org]] |access-date=March 25, 2025}}
|{{cite web |publisher=[[Computer History Museum]] |title=Oral History of Lois Jennings Britton |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QPuSZlcieN4 |website=[[YouTube]] |date=July 5, 2023}}}}</ref>

Brand met Ryan Phelan when she applied for a job to work at ''Whole Earth Catalog'', and the two married in 1983.<ref>{{cite web |title=Revive & Restore (2012– ) |url=https://embryo.asu.edu/pages/revive-restore-2012 |website=embryo.asu.edu {{!}} Embryo Project Encyclopedia |access-date=March 25, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Seligman |first1=Katherine |title=The Social Entrepreneur / Ryan Phelan's controversial new venture is part of her quest to make life questions – whether about our DNA or the species' existence – easier for the rest of us |url=https://www.sfgate.com/magazine/article/The-Social-Entrepreneur-Ryan-Phelan-s-2544385.php |access-date=March 25, 2025 |work=[[SFGATE]] |date=January 8, 2006}}</ref> The couple lives on ''Mirene'', a {{convert|64|ft|adj=on}}-long working [[tugboat]]. Built in 1912, the boat is moored in a former shipyard in [[Sausalito, California]].<ref name="Lewine">{{cite news|last=Lewine|first=Edward|author-link=Edward Lewine|title=On the Waterfront|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/04/19/magazine/19wwln-domains-t.html|date=April 19, 2009|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=November 2, 2009}}</ref> He works in ''Mary Heartline'', a grounded fishing boat about 100 yards (90 metres) away.<ref name="Lewine" /> One of his favorite items is a table on which [[Otis Redding]] is said to have written "[[(Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay]]", a furnishing that Brand acquired from an antiques dealer in Sausalito.<ref name="Lewine" />

==USCO and Merry Pranksters==
By the mid-1960s, Brand became associated with New York multimedia group [[USCO]] and Bay Area author [[Ken Kesey]] and his [[Merry Pranksters]]. Brand co-produced the [[Acid Tests#Trips Festival|1966 Trips Festival]], an early effort blending rock music and [[Liquid light shows|light shows]], with Kesey and [[Ramón Sender Barayón]]. The Trips Festival was among the first [[Grateful Dead]] performances in San Francisco. An estimated 10,000 [[hippies]] attended, and [[Haight-Ashbury]] soon emerged as the epicenter of an emerging counterculture, with the [[Summer of Love]] in 1967.<ref>{{cite video|people=Brand, Stewart|title=From Counterculture to Cyberculture: The Legacy of the Whole Earth Catalog|url=http://video.google.com/videoplay?docid=-9001613451407405270#|publisher=Stanford University Libraries via Google|time=32:30|access-date=November 7, 2009}}</ref> [[Tom Wolfe]] includes Brand in his 1968 book ''[[The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test]]''.<ref>Wolfe, T., ''The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test'' (New York: [[Farrar, Straus and Giroux]], 1968), [https://books.google.com/books?id=Ejf6Ql1F6_gC&pg=PT363 pp. 363 ff.]</ref>

==NASA images of Earth==
[[File:ATSIII 10NOV67 153107.jpg|thumb|Earth from space, by [[ATS-3]] satellite, 1967]]
[[File:NASA-Apollo8-Dec24-Earthrise.jpg|thumb|''[[Earthrise]]'', by [[William Anders]], [[Apollo 8]], 1968]]
{{See also|The Blue Marble}}

In 1966, while on an [[Lysergic acid diethylamide|LSD]] trip on the roof of his house in [[North Beach, San Francisco]], Brand became convinced that seeing an image of the whole Earth would change how we think about the planet and ourselves.<ref>{{Cite news|author=David Honigmann|title=Lunch with the FT: Stewart Brand|url=https://www.ft.com/content/652828ec-fbe0-11de-9c29-00144feab49a|newspaper=[[Financial Times]]|date=January 9, 2010|archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20221210/https://www.ft.com/content/652828ec-fbe0-11de-9c29-00144feab49a |archive-date=December 10, 2022 |url-access=subscription|access-date=May 22, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=Profile: Stewart Brand |url=http://www.theguardian.com/education/2001/aug/04/artsandhumanities.highereducation |date=August 3, 2001 |newspaper=[[The Guardian]] |access-date=May 22, 2020}}</ref> He then campaigned to have [[NASA]] release the then-rumored satellite image of the entire Earth as seen from space. He sold and distributed buttons for 25 cents each,<ref name="Brand-Smithsonian">{{cite web|author=Brand, Stewart|title=Photography changes our relationship to our planet |url=http://click.si.edu/Story.aspx?story=31 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080530221651/http://click.si.edu/Story.aspx?story=31 |url-status=dead |archive-date=May 30, 2008 |publisher=Smithsonian Photography Initiative |access-date=November 6, 2009}}</ref> asking, "Why haven't we seen a photograph of the whole Earth yet?"<ref name="Brand-214">{{harvnb|Brand|2009|p=214}}</ref> During this campaign, Brand met [[Richard Buckminster Fuller]], who offered to help Brand with his projects.<ref>{{cite web|author=Leonard, Jennifer|title=Stewart Brand on the long view|url=http://www.renegademedia.info/books/stewart-brand.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071212213039/http://www.renegademedia.info/books/stewart-brand.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=December 12, 2007|access-date=February 5, 2013}}</ref>

In 1967, the [[ATS-3]] satellite took the photo Brand had envisioned. He thought the image of our planet would be a powerful symbol and featured it on the first (fall 1968) edition of the ''[[Whole Earth Catalog]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.wholeearth.com/uploads/2/Image/covers/thumbs-md/md-fall-1968-1010-cover.jpg|title=The front cover of the Fall 1968 edition of the ''Whole Earth Catalog'' showing the AST-3 image of 10 November 1967|website=wholeearth.com}}</ref> Later in 1968, NASA astronaut [[Bill Anders]] took an Earth photo,<ref name="Brand-214" /> ''[[Earthrise]]'', from Moon orbit, which became the front image of the spring 1969 edition of the ''Catalog''. 1970 saw the first celebration of [[Earth Day]].<ref name="Brand-Smithsonian" />

==Douglas Engelbart==
In late 1968, Brand assisted electrical engineer [[Douglas Engelbart]] with [[the Mother of All Demos]], a presentation of many revolutionary computer technologies (including [[hypertext]], email, and the [[Computer mouse|mouse]]) to the [[Fall Joint Computer Conference]] in San Francisco.<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Fisher |first1=Adam |title=How Doug Engelbart Pulled off the Mother of All Demos |url=https://www.wired.com/story/how-doug-engelbart-pulled-off-the-mother-of-all-demos/ |access-date=December 12, 2018 |magazine=Wired |date=December 9, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | last=O'Mara | first=Margaret Pugh | title=The code : Silicon Valley and the remaking of America | publisher=Penguin Press | publication-place=New York | year=2020 | isbn=978-0-399-56220-4 | oclc=1176354772 | page=128}}</ref>

Brand surmised that given the necessary consciousness, information, and tools, human beings could reshape the world they had made (and were making) for themselves into something environmentally and socially sustainable.<ref name="Kirk">{{cite book|author=Kirk, Andrew G.|title=Counterculture Green: The Whole Earth Catalog and American Environmentalism|year=2007|publisher=University Press of Kansas |isbn=978-0-7006-1545-2}}</ref>{{rp|42}}

==''Whole Earth Catalog ''==
During the late 1960s and early 1970s, about 10&nbsp;million Americans were involved in living [[Intentional community|communally]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=From counterculture to cyberculture : Stewart Brand, the Whole Earth Network, and the rise of digital utopianism|last=Turner, Fred.|date=2006|publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=0226817415|location=Chicago|oclc=62533774}}</ref> In 1968, using the most basic approaches to [[typesetting]] and page layout, Brand and his colleagues created issue number one of the ''[[Whole Earth Catalog]]'', with the subtitle "access to tools".<ref name="Kirk" /> {{rp|48}} The Portola Institute provided financial support for Brand's brainchild.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Markoff |first1=John |title=Access to Success |url=https://www.altaonline.com/dispatches/a4127/access-to-success/ |website=Alta |date=November 22, 2018 |access-date=October 2, 2024}}</ref> Until 1980, editions of the ''Whole Earth Catalog'' were published by the Portola Institute.<ref name="Wiener" /> Brand and his wife, Lois, traveled to communes in a 1963 Dodge truck known as the ''Whole Earth Truck Store'', which (as a division of the Portola Institute) moved to a storefront in [[Menlo Park, California]].<ref name="Kirk" />{{rp|48}}

The first oversized ''Catalog'', and its successors from the 1970s to the last issue (in 1994), included a wide assortment of things that could serve as useful "tools": books, maps, garden implements, specialized clothing, carpenters' and [[Brick mason|masons]]' tools, forestry gear, tents, welding equipment, professional journals, early synthesizers, and personal computers. It also comprised ideas, stories, examples of successful projects, mentors like [[Buckminster Fuller]], and the experiences of many pioneers. The catalog anticipated social media by reflecting its readers' contemporary experiences in the world. Brand invited "reviews" (written in the form of a letter to a friend) of the best of these items from experts in specific fields or from ordinary people with experience. The catalog described where these things could be located or purchased, if they could be, or how they could be created. Its publication coincided with the wave of social and cultural experimentation, convention-breaking, and "[[do it yourself]]" attitude associated with the [[Counterculture of the 1960s|counterculture]].{{Citation needed|date=April 2026}}

The ''Whole Earth Catalog'' had widespread influence within the rural [[back-to-the-land movement]] of the 1970s, and the communities movement within many cities throughout the United States, Canada, and Australia. The 1972 edition sold 1.5&nbsp;million copies, winning the first U.S.&nbsp;[[National Book Award]] in the [[List of winners of the National Book Award#Current|Contemporary Affairs]] category.<ref>[https://www.nationalbook.org/awards-prizes/national-book-awards-1972 "National Book Awards – 1972"]. [[National Book Foundation]]. Retrieved March 9, 2012. (There was a "Contemporary" or "Current" award category from 1972 to 1980.)</ref>

[[Steve Jobs]] ended his 2005 commencement address at [[Stanford University]] by acknowledging both Stewart Brand and the ''Whole Earth Catalog'', quoting its farewell message: "Stay hungry. Stay foolish".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://news.stanford.edu/2005/06/14/jobs-061505/ |title='You've got to find what you love', Jobs says |date=June 14, 2005 |publisher=Stanford University|access-date=March 1, 2021}}</ref><ref>Archived at [https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211211/UF8uR6Z6KLc Ghostarchive]{{cbignore}} and the [https://web.archive.org/web/20080507103244/http://youtube.com:80/watch?v=UF8uR6Z6KLc Wayback Machine]{{cbignore}}: {{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UF8uR6Z6KLc |title=Steve Jobs' 2005 Stanford Commencement Address |date=2009 |publisher=Stanford University|access-date=March 1, 2021}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

==''CoEvolution Quarterly''==
{{More citations needed section|date=November 2025}}
[[File:Stewart Brand with passenger pigeon study specimens.jpg|thumb|Brand with [[passenger pigeon]] [[study skins]]]]
To continue his work and also to publish full-length articles on specific topics in the natural sciences and invention, in numerous areas of the arts and the [[social sciences]], and on the contemporary scene in general, Brand founded ''[[CoEvolution Quarterly]]'' in 1974, aimed primarily at educated laypeople.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Counterculture Green: The Whole Earth Catalog and American Environmentalism |last=Kirk |first=Andrew G. |pages=88–90, 100, 165–166 |year=2007 |publication-place=Lawrence, KS |publisher=University Press of Kansas |isbn=978-0-7006-1821-7}}</ref> Brand never better revealed his opinions and reason for hope than when he ran, in ''CoEvolution Quarterly'' #4, a transcription of technology historian [[Lewis Mumford]]'s talk "The Next Transformation of Man", in which he stated that "man has still within him sufficient resources to alter the direction of modern civilization, for we then need no longer regard man as the passive victim of his own irreversible technological development".<ref>Mumford, Lewis "Enough Energy for Life & the Next Transformation of Man" ''CoEvolution Quarterly'' issue 4, 1974-12-21, pp 19–23.</ref>

The content of ''CoEvolution Quarterly'' often included [[futurism]] or risqué topics. Besides giving space to unknown writers with something to say, Brand presented articles by many respected authors and thinkers, including Mumford, [[Howard T. Odum]], [[Witold Rybczynski]], [[Karl Hess]], [[Orville Schell]], [[Ivan Illich]], [[Wendell Berry]], [[Ursula K. Le Guin]], [[Gregory Bateson]], [[Amory Lovins]], [[Hazel Henderson]], [[Gary Snyder]], [[Lynn Margulis]], [[Eric Drexler]], [[Gerard K. O'Neill]], [[Peter Calthorpe]], [[Sim Van der Ryn]], [[Paul Hawken]], [[John Todd (Canadian biologist)|John Todd]], [[Kevin Kelly (editor)|Kevin Kelly]], and [[Donella Meadows]]. In the ensuing years, Brand authored and edited a number of books on topics as diverse as computer-based media, the life history of buildings, and ideas about [[Space colonization|space colonies]].

In 1984, Brand founded the ''[[Whole Earth Software Catalog and Review|Whole Earth Software Review]]'', a supplement to the ''Whole Earth Software Catalog''. It was merged with ''CoEvolution Quarterly'' to form the ''[[Whole Earth Review]]'' in 1985.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Turner |first1=Fred |title=From Counterculture to Cyberculture: Stewart Brand, the Whole Earth Network, and the Rise of Digital Utopianism |date=2008 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |location=Chicago, Illinois |pages=129–130}}</ref>

==California government==
From 1977 to 1979, Brand served as "special advisor" to the administration of California Governor [[Jerry Brown]].<ref>"Governor of California, BallotPedia, https://ballotpedia.org/Jerry_Brown_(California)</ref><ref name="brandlife" />

==The WELL==
In 1985, Brand and [[Larry Brilliant]] founded [[the WELL]] ("Whole Earth 'Lectronic Link"), a prototypical, wide-ranging online community for informed participants the world over.<ref>{{Cite book|title=From counterculture to cyberculture: Stewart Brand, the Whole Earth Network, and the rise of digital utopianism |last=Fred |first=Turner |date=2006 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |isbn=0226817415 |location=Chicago|oclc=62533774}}</ref><!-- Image with inadequate rationale removed: [[File:Well logo.gif|right]] --> The WELL won the 1990 Best Online Publication Award from the [[Computer Press Association]].<ref>Katie Hafner, ''The WELL: A Story of Love, Death and Real Life in the Seminal Online Community'':(2001) Carroll & Graf Publishers {{ISBN|0-7867-0846-8}}</ref>

==All Species Foundation==
In 2000, Brand helped launch the [[All Species Foundation]],<ref name="kelly-bio">{{cite web |last1=Kelly |first1=Kevin |title=Biography |url=https://kk.org/biography |website=Kevin Kelly |access-date=July 28, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190518095911/https://kk.org/biography/ |archive-date=May 18, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Hitt|first=Jack|author-link=Jack Hitt|title= The year in ideas: A to Z; The All-Species Inventory |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/12/09/magazine/the-year-in-ideas-a-to-z-the-all-species-inventory.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=July 28, 2019 |date=December 9, 2001}}</ref> which aimed to catalog all species of life on Earth.<ref>{{cite web |title=A Call for the Discovery of All Life-Forms on Earth |url=http://www.all-species.org/call.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070202032924/http://www.all-species.org/call.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=February 2, 2007 |website=All Species Foundation |access-date=July 28, 2019}}</ref> The project ceased functioning in 2007, transferring its mission to the ''[[Encyclopedia of Life]]''.<ref name="kelly-bio" />

==Global Business Network==
[[File:Frontiers Cocnert Nov 2010-0491 (5155112565).jpg|thumb|Brand speaking at the Frontiers Conference, 2010]]
[[File:Stewart Brand (49624953803).jpg|thumb|Brand in 2020]]

During 1986, Brand was a visiting scientist at the [[MIT Media Lab]]. Soon after, he became a private-conference organizer for such corporations as [[Royal Dutch Shell]], [[Volvo]], and [[AT&T Corporation|AT&T]]. In 1988, he became a co‑founder of the [[Global Business Network]], which became involved with the evolution and application of [[scenario thinking]], planning, and complementary strategic tools.<ref name="Wiener" /> For fourteen years, Brand was on the board of the [[Santa Fe Institute]] (founded in 1984), an organization devoted to "fostering a [[Academic discipline#Multidisciplinary|multidisciplinary]] scientific research community pursuing frontier science". He has also continued to promote the preservation of tracts of wilderness.

==''Whole Earth Discipline''==
The ''Whole Earth Catalog'' implied an ideal of human [[progress (history)|progress]] that depended on decentralized, personal, and liberating technological development—so‑called "soft technology". However, in 2005, Brand criticized aspects of the international environmental ideology he had helped to develop. He wrote an article called "Environmental Heresies"<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.technologyreview.com/s/404000/environmental-heresies/|title=Environmental Heresies|work=MIT Technology Review}}</ref> in the May 2005 issue of the [[MIT]] ''[[Technology Review]]'', in which he described what he considered necessary changes to environmentalism. He suggested, among other things, that environmentalists embrace [[nuclear power]] and [[genetically modified organisms]] as technologies with more promise than risk.<ref name="Wiener">{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.newyorker.com/news/letter-from-silicon-valley/the-complicated-legacy-of-stewart-brands-whole-earth-catalog|title=The Complicated Legacy of Stewart Brand's ''Whole Earth Catalog''|last=Wiener|first=Anna|author-link=Anna Wiener|date=November 16, 2018|magazine=[[The New Yorker]]|access-date=May 18, 2019}}</ref>

Brand later developed these ideas into a book and published ''[[Whole Earth Discipline|Whole Earth Discipline: An Ecopragmatist Manifesto]]'' in 2009. The book examines how urbanization, nuclear power, [[genetic engineering]], [[climate engineering|geoengineering]], and wildlife restoration can be used as powerful tools in humanity's ongoing fight against [[global warming]].<ref name="whole-earth-discipline">{{cite book|title=Whole Earth Discipline: An Ecopragmatist Manifesto|title-link=Whole Earth Discipline|first=Stewart|last=Brand|publisher=Viking|year=2009|isbn=978-0-670-02121-5}}</ref>

In a 2019 interview, Brand described his perspective as "post-libertarian", indicating that at the time when the ''Whole Earth Catalog'' was being written, he did not fully understand the significance of the role of government in the development of technology and engineering.<ref name="Wiener" /> In his environmental position, he self-describes as an "eco-pragmatist".<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/03/25/books/review/whole-earth-john-markoff.html | title=Stewart Brand's Long, Strange Trip | newspaper=[[The New York Times]]| date=March 25, 2022 | last=Sabin | first=Paul}}</ref>

==Long Now Foundation==
Brand is co‑chair and president of the board of directors of the [[Long Now Foundation]] and chairs the foundation's [[Seminars About Long-term Thinking]]. This series on long-term thinking has presented a range of speakers, including [[Brian Eno]], [[Neal Stephenson]], [[Vernor Vinge]], [[Philip Rosedale]], [[Jimmy Wales]], [[Kevin Kelly (editor)|Kevin Kelly]], [[Clay Shirky]], [[Ray Kurzweil]], [[Bruce Sterling]], and [[Cory Doctorow]]. The Long Now Foundation has worked with [[Jeff Bezos]] to build the [[10,000 Year Clock]].<ref>{{cite web | website=Fox News | date=December 15, 2023 | title=''Inside mountain where billionaire Jeff Bezos is building clock that will last longer than us'' | url=https://www.foxnews.com/tech/inside-the-mountain-where-billionaire-jeff-bezos-is-building-as-clock-last-longer-than-us | access-date=August 25, 2024}}</ref>

Brand is the subject of the 2021 documentary film ''[[We Are As Gods (film)|We Are As Gods]]''.<ref>{{cite news| last=Marsh | first=Calum | title=''We Are as Gods'' review: Turn On, Tune in, Drop Out |newspaper=[[The New York Times]]| date=September 6, 2022 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/09/06/movies/we-are-as-gods-review.html | access-date=January 30, 2024}}</ref>

==Works==
'''Stewart Brand''' is the initiator or was involved with the development of the following:
* ''[[Whole Earth Catalog]]'' in 1968
* ''[[CoEvolution Quarterly]]'' in 1974
* ''[[Whole Earth Software Catalog and Review]]'' in 1984
* ''[[Whole Earth Review]]'' in 1985
* [[Point Foundation (environment)|Point Foundation]]
* [[Global Business Network]] (co-founder)<ref name="Wiener" />
* [[The WELL]] in 1985, with [[Larry Brilliant]]
* [[The Hackers Conference]] in 1984
* [[Long Now Foundation]] in 1996, with computer scientist [[Danny Hillis]]—one of the foundation's projects is to build a 10,000 year clock, the [[Clock of the Long Now]]
* ''[[The New Games Book|New Games Tournament]]'' (was involved initially but left the project)
* In April 2015, Brand joined with a group of scholars in issuing ''[[An Ecomodernist Manifesto]]''.<ref>{{cite web|title=An Ecomodernist Manifesto|url=http://www.ecomodernism.org/manifesto/|website=ecomodernism.org|access-date=April 17, 2015|quote=A good Anthropocene demands that humans use their growing social, economic, and technological powers to make life better for people, stabilize the climate, and protect the natural world.}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=Eduardo Porter|title=A Call to Look Past Sustainable Development|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/04/15/business/an-environmentalist-call-to-look-past-sustainable-development.html|access-date=April 17, 2015|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=April 14, 2015|quote=On Tuesday, a group of scholars involved in the environmental debate, including Professor Roy and Professor Brook, Ruth DeFries of Columbia University, and Michael Shellenberger and Ted Nordhaus of the Breakthrough Institute in Oakland, Calif., issued what they are calling the "Eco-modernist Manifesto".}}</ref> The other authors included: [[Barry Brook (scientist)|Barry Brook]], [[Ruth DeFries]], [[Erle Ellis]], [[David Keith (scientist)|David Keith]], [[Mark Lynas]], [[Ted Nordhaus]], [[Roger A. Pielke Jr.]], [[Michael Shellenberger]], and [[Robert Stone (director)|Robert Stone]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Authors an Ecomodernist Manifesto|url=http://www.ecomodernism.org/authors/|website=ecomodernism.org|access-date=April 17, 2015|quote=As scholars, scientists, campaigners, and citizens, we write with the conviction that knowledge and technology, applied with wisdom, might allow for a good, or even great, [[Anthropocene]].}}</ref>
